nodes.title: Caching reduces page load time
nodes.body: Top-level claim this demo graph is organized around: serving cached responses from an edge node should noticeably cut perceived load time for read-heavy traffic.

nodes.title: Edge cache cuts median TTFB by >30%
nodes.body: A testable, falsifiable version of the claim: caching at the edge reduces median time-to-first-byte by more than 30% relative to an uncached baseline, for our current traffic mix.

nodes.title: Traffic is read-heavy (>90% GET requests)
nodes.body: Caching only helps if most requests are cacheable reads. If the real traffic mix is write-heavy, the hypothesis doesn't even apply.

nodes.title: A/B load test: cached vs. uncached edge
nodes.body: Concrete experiment that evaluates N002: run identical synthetic load against a cached and an uncached edge configuration and compare TTFB distributions.

nodes.title: Staging benchmark: 42% TTFB reduction
nodes.body: Result of N004. See the attached document for the full benchmark methodology and numbers.

nodes.title: Cache invalidation lag can serve stale prices
nodes.body: A way N001/N002 can break in practice: if invalidation lags a price change, customers can see stale (wrong) prices for the TTL window. Needs its own test before this is shipped for pricing-sensitive pages.

nodes.title: TTFB reduction, measured in milliseconds
nodes.body: Operationalizes "page load time" from N001 into something we can actually measure: time-to-first-byte in ms, median and p99.

nodes.title: Ship edge caching for read-only pages only
nodes.body: Given N005's result and the open risk in N006, ship caching for pages with no pricing/inventory data first, and gate pricing pages behind a fix for the invalidation-lag failure mode.

edges.rationale: The hypothesis only makes sense if the traffic is actually read-heavy enough for caching to matter.
This is the concrete experiment that evaluates the hypothesis.
Benchmark result from running N004: 42% median TTFB reduction supports the >30% hypothesis.
Turns the vague "load time" claim into a concrete, measurable quantity.
Pricing pages are the case where this claim breaks down without an invalidation fix.
A confirmed hypothesis is the main support for the top-level claim.
The decision to ship leans directly on the benchmark evidence.
The decision explicitly carves out the failure mode rather than ignoring it.
